utterances.text: So if that can be done, it will be much appreciated. We will hear from you once you have discussed amongst yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And that concludes the presentation, Your Honour. I would ask that Mr. Cannata and I be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suppose we are having a new team for the Prosecution. It might, perhaps, place itself on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, for the balance of the afternoon, Barney Thomas, Lorna Bolton, April Carter, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Madam Carter will be leading the next witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Good afternoon, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. May it please the Court, the Prosecution calls Witness Nedzib, Dozo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. May you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dozo. You may sit down. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, will you please introduce yourself to the Court.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: My name is Dozo Nedzib. I was born on 4th of May, 1958, in the place called Batina, Pale municipality, Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: During the war what job did you hold?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, were you involved in the war at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the war broke out, I came to the police station in the Stari Grad municipality where I worked as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Prior to today, you have testify in the Dragomir Milosevic case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And, for the record, Your Honour, the transcript of that testimony of 14 March 2007 bears the 65 ter number 9422. On Monday, your transcript was read back to you in a language you understood. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And you indicated that you had a few clarifications to that transcript. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Specifically, you indicated at page 3680, line 21, where the name D-a-r-t-e-l-j-e was incorrect, and it should read D-a-t-e-l-j-i. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You also indicated that you did not understand the translation at page 3686, line 2, in which the English reads "to the house that was shown us where billed Selmanovic." However, you were satisfied with the further question and answer that that was clarified. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You also indicated at page 3688, line 22, that the word "G-o-r-d-o-n-j" was incorrect and should be "G-r-d-o-n-j-a." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Lastly you indicated at page 3690 at line 3, the term "line of sight" should have read "line of fire." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: After those clarifications, if you were asked those same questions today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter number 9422 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1936, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Within that transcript, several exhibits were tendered through you. First of all, your statement of 22 November 1995 was admitted as P363, at page 3683, with clarifications regarding paragraph 8. With that clarification, do you adopt that same statement here today?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter number 9420 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, do we have the clarifications? Are we going to be able see the clarifications when we look at the statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the clarifications are actually made within the body of the D. Milosevic transcript on that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you were talking here about clarifications to P363 which is his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: 363 is his statement. However when they tendered it as a 92 ter package within the D. Milosevic case, they provided clarification within the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What are we admitting? Are we admitting P363 of Milosevic as an exhibit here? Or do have you a 65 ter number for this?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The 65 ter in this case is 9420.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 9420. And you have tendered it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1937, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Further, your statement of 21 April 2005 was admitted as P364, and that was done, again, at page 3683. However, during your proofing on Monday, you indicated that had you a clarification to make with regards to paragraph 8. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Specifically, you indicated that that paragraph should be fully redacted. And in its place it should read: "In August 1995, I heard a shell hit a street. A shell makes a different sound when it hits a street rather than a building. Moments later I arrived at the police station in Stari Grad which was 30 to 40 metres away. My supervisor advised me that a shell hit outside Markale market. "Two or three cars from the station went to the market to transport the wounded. The market is outside our station's area, so I was not involved in the technical investigation. I may have gone to the market to assist at a later time, but all wounded had already been taken away before I arrived. Later, we watched television footage of the dead and wounded. I took some follow-up statements at a later date." And I do apologise, Your Honour, I identified that as being a replacement for paragraph 8. That should actually be a replacement for paragraph 5. Sir, with that clarification made, do you adopt that statement here today?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I tender 65 ter number 9421 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1938, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Lastly, the on-site investigation report of 14 December 1994 was also admitted as P367 at page 3693. Do you adopt that report as well here today?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 65 ter number 8614 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1939, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Before turning to the direct examination, I will read out a summary of the witness's evidence: Since 1992 Nedzib Dozo has been a police officer serving in the old town area of Sarajevo known as Stari Grad. His evidence is related to his investigation into a large number of crimes, including sniping and shelling incidents, as well as air bombs. Mr. Dozo will provide specific evidence related to the sniping incident B-9 of 10 December 1994, where civilians were fired upon from Spicaste, S-p-i-c-a-s-t-a; second word, Stijena, S-t-i-j-e-n-a; as well as the shelling incident A-4 of 22 December 1994, where two shells landed in a flea market; as well as investigations of shelling predating but relating to the shelling incident A-9 of 28 August 1995, colloquially known as Markale II.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, the last exhibit that we discussed with regard to your Dragomir Milosevic testimony related to incident B-9 where an on-site investigation was performed relating to a sniping victim, Dervisa Selmanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a bit taken by surprise because we thought that this witness was a 92 ter witness, so unless there is some special reasons there should be any examination-in-chief. My learned friend has not explained why she wants to examine in chief this witness, so I wonder whether there is some deviation from the rule that is well established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as Defence I'm sure is aware, we have actually requested for an hour and a half of life testimony to be taken from this witness in order to take clarifications and highlighting of certain aspects of his testimony. We will be asking questions in relation to all three incidents which are not contained within his 92 ter materials. And we believe that it would assist the Court in the final determination of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. In relation to certain witnesses, when the Prosecution wanted to have examination-in-chief, they requested that their status be changed from 92 ter to viva voce witnesses. And if this witness is now examined in chief, that means that his status has been changed, and we have not been inform about this. As far as we know, this witness came as a 92 ter witness. We have received material and his previous testimony, transcript of it, and that's what we were expecting. This is a complete surprise for us now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, paragraph 21 of our guidelines, you have complied with, and it doesn't look to me like unless you have made prior arrangements with your colleagues you have any further rights to lead the witness. I beg your pardon, sorry, I apologise. Mr. Lukic, the same paragraph, does allow her to do a limited examination to clarify or highlight particular aspects of the statement. So she would be allowed to do so. You may proceed, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to advise the Chamber as well that on 26 September 2008 when we tendered the submission a revised witness list with confidential Annex A, witness Dozo was listed as number 76 as a 92 ter witness, but we specifically indicated that the estimated hours of examination-in-chief was one half hours. So I just want to clarify that for the record since Defence counsel had indicated that they had no prior warning that this witness would be led live. And I will continue with my examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to address first incident B-9 that took place in December of 1994. You provided in your previous transcript an on-site investigation report of 14 December 1994. When you originally came on-site who was providing information with regards to the sniping of Dervisa Selmanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: As far as for the manner of shooting and the location of it, we were informed about it by the neighbours of Mrs. Selmanovic. The locals. When this incident took place, they managed to get her out from the area where she had been wounded to pull her out of it. And then with the help of UNPROFOR, they transported her to the Kosevo Hospital where she was admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At some later point, did you have an opportunity to speak with Ms. Dervisa Selmanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: That day when that incident happened when she was wounded, I didn't manage to talk to her, to interview her on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to interview her on any day?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, three months later, approximately three months later. It was only then that we managed to locate her because she had moved out of the house where she resided to another municipality, to Centar municipality. And it wasn't until three months later that we managed to locate her.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would ask for 65 ter 8614 to be brought up into e-court. My apologies, Your Honour. Actually, it should be 65 ter 2640.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the document before you?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What is the document?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: This is an Official Note, after the interview with Ms. Selmanovic, which was drawn up by myself, and I sent it on to the police station, and from there, it went to the relevant unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And just for clarity of the record, within the December 1994 report it was indicated that her left leg was shot. However, in the 1995 report, it said it was her right. Can you please explain this difference.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The day that she was wounded I was duty police officer in the police station, and the head of the shift was called by residents who told him that there was some shooting from Spicaste Stijena, as a result of which a female person was wounded. Later on we learned that it was Mrs. Selmanovic. Also, the person who reported the incident to the police station said that she had been wounded in her left leg. Since neither I nor the on-site investigation team managed to talk to Mrs. Selmanovic, because we hadn't been able to locate her, we simply noted that down, based on what we had heard from the neighbours, who also said that she had been wounded in the left leg. I guess they were scared, under stress, and that's what they reported to us. Later on, when I managed to locate her and find where she lived, we interviewed her, and it turned out she said to us and it was also supported by the doctor's report that she had been wounded in her right leg. And this is what we wrote down in the Official Note then.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I would now like to move on to the incident A-4, which was the shelling incident of the flea market on 22 December 1994. Did you take part in that investigation?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. As a member of the on-site investigation team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Sorry I am still having some problems here. So my mind has taken -- Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, once again, I will reiterate my previous objection, with another explanation. All of the questions that we have heard so far from my learned friend have been covered in previous testimonies and statements. We haven't heard anything new, in addition to what can be filed in the 92 ter package. If the Prosecutor wants an explanation in accordance with Rule 21, they need to precede each of their questions with the explanation of what it is that they're exactly seeking from the witness that is in addition to the 92 ter package. If you were to look at the 92 ter package, you would see that everything that has been elicited from the witness so far is included in that package. There is nothing new. No new information there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not clear what package the Defence counsel is reviewing. There were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Reviewing the 92 ter package. That's what he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And if he were, the fact that the exhibit that I just tendered is not found within the 92 ter package, would indicate that this is in fact new information. I will concede that there is an aspect where there was some discussion within the portions of the package, specifically the transcript, where the left leg/right leg difference was noted; however, because dealing with a new exhibit that was not addressed within that old package. I felt that I needed to clarify and to highlight that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But this confusion about which leg was injured, was it not -- is it not already contained in the -- in the 92 ter package?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Very minimally, Your Honour. And because there is no citation to the 1995 report in the 92 ter package, I felt in order to have a complete record, we needed to relate the two documents to each other and this would be how we would do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Notwithstanding that you gave notice to your colleagues that you are going to lead this witness for one and a half hours, the rule gives you limited leading. You are still subject to limited leading. You may not necessarily have the entire one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, were you a part of the investigation of the shelling of the flea market on 22 December 1994?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the team.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would ask that 65 ter 1439B be brought up into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do that, was 2640 admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honour. I did not ask for 2640 to be tendered. I do so now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 2640 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1940, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, it is break time. Would it be a convenient if we took a break and let the technician work on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the break I determined that I'm going to re-order the testimony, and so I'd now like to move on to testimony related to scheduled incident A-9, and I would ask that 65 ter number 9244.01 be brought up into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you abandoning 1439B?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: For the time being, Your Honour. I will pick it up again later. Can this exhibit be expanded to full screen. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, that has been admitted as P1938, you refer to several investigations related to shellings that predated the Markale II incident of August 1995. I would ask you to look at the exhibit that's before you. Do you recognise the area depicted in this map?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. This is one part of the so-called old town and one part of the so-called Centar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. With the assistance of the usher, I would ask you to make a few markings on this map. Can you first mark on the map the market which was hit on 5 February 1994. And when you locate it, if you can mark it with A-3.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. In addition, can you also please mark the market that was hit on 28 August 1995 and mark that with an A-9.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: It's very close some 50 to 100 metres away from this place, in the same street.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to have a screen shot taken of this image and it be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1941, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to elaborate on paragraph 9 of that -- of your 1995 statement, in relation to the same map. You indicated that there was a single shelling that took place on a day near Markale market. Can you just tell us when exactly did this shelling take place, the singular one?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Which particular shelling are you referring to? Or are you talking about Markale II or Markale 1?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm -- in reference to your statement, you indicated that there was one incident where there was a single shelling and another incident where there was three shellings that came in quick succession. I want to deal first with the shelling that took place individually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe my learned friend should refer to a particular paragraph in the statement. That would allow the witness to understand the question, because some things may be lost in translation. So maybe my learned friend should go to the statement and refer the witness to the paragraph in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... understand the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. May I? May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. Can you please tell me when did the singular incident take place in relation to the August 28th Markale market shelling?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Before Markale II, which was on 28 August -- or, rather, that incident happened in the morning, around 11.00, 11.30, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which incident is it? The one of the 28th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I think things are getting lost in translation, sir. Okay. I'm not talking about the Markale II incident. But there are two paragraphs in Exhibit P1938, in which you indicate: "To begin, there's something more interesting to tell. I was part of the investigation team that investigated some shellings short before the big shelling of Markale on 28 August 1995." So I want to talk about those investigations. Now you have broken it up in your statement between two separate periods: One with three shellings, one with a singular shelling. I want to start with the one that is a singular shelling. Can you please tell me when that singular shelling took place.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact day when that happened, but it was before the Markale II shelling. I went for an on-site inspection, in the immediate vicinity of the street -- or, rather, the Markale market, and we were able to establish that two or three shells had been fired from the area known as Barice in the north. The shells fell on the Geneta [phoen] Cikma Street across the street from the Markale market. Two or three children fell victim. I'm not sure how many. Actually, I don't know whether any of them died. However, everything pointed to the fact that the shells had been fired in the direction of the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, I understand that you can't give me a specific date, but can you tell me was it within a year, within six months, within a month, within weeks? Can you give us some approximation?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Approximately a month before that shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would actually like to have P1941 with the markings that the witness made on screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Doesn't look like the markings are still there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If they're not, I can certainly undergo the exercise again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What did you want to do with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to have the witness identify where the shelling landed that injured these children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you're going to give it another number.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And with the help of the usher, sir, can you please identify on this map where the children were injured that you just spoke of?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I see that you have drawn a bit of a star figure just above A-3. Are you indicating that that's the location where the children were injured? If I can get a verbal response, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then can you please mark that star with a C.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd ask a screen shot be taken of this image and it be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1942, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, through the investigations of that event, did you determine what the direction of fire was?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. It was established that the shells had arrived from the direction north, from the settlements of Barice and Mrkovici or rather the neighbourhoods with those names.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who controlled that area?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to bring P1941 back on screen. And we're going turn now to the series of three shellings that took place. Sir, did the series of three shellings happen on the same day as the shelling that we were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No, not on the same day. It was either before or after, one or two days before or after, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you said that three shells -- there were three shellings that day. Can you please describe what was hit with the first shelling?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The first shell exploded in the street that was once called something, and I don't remember what it was called, but nowadays it is Skenderija Street, very close to a bridge and very close to a secondary school that is located there. And I know that one young man died there. He was a student at the school of political sciences.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Do you see the location where the student was hit on the map before you?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would ask that, in a different colour, you place a number 1 where the student was killed, or injured, pardon.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You also indicated that there was a second shelling. Can you please describe what was hit during the second shelling?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The second shell hit the then JNA street, as it was known then, and today it is known as the defender of Sarajevo street. In front of the building of the Stari Grad municipality. I don't know whether anybody was killed there. I know that there were several wounded. Among them there was a foreigner who was an employee of a humanitarian or a charitable organisation that was, at the time, involved in the installation of gas pipes in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would ask you to place a number 2 where these men were injured.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated there was a third shelling on that day. What occurred at that shelling?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The third shell fell in Mula Mustafe Baseskije Street, which was then known as Marsal Tito Street. And it hit the wall of the so-called Konzum building. It was a food store. I know for sure that one person was killed, that several persons were wounded on that occasion. And I know that the person who was killed by the shell, the situation was rather gruesome. We found a complete brain scattered on the street after the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please mark with a 3 the location of this shelling?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And I would ask that a screen shot be taken of this exhibit and it be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1943, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I will be asking with no further markings. The rest will be led with the testimony. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please advise us how close to the Markale market was the third shelling?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The third shell fell not more than 30 metres away from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And how far did the second shell fall from the third shell?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The first shell fell in the Suceska Street, the next one in the JNA street, and the distance between the two is about 100 metres, and the third shell fell at about the same distance to the previous two.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand the last answer [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I will clarify, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll just start again from the first shell. How far was the first shell to Markale?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The first shell hit a place up to 250 or 300 metres away from Markale, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And how close was the second shelling to Markale?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The shells fell at a distance of some 100 metres from each other. The second shell hit a place that was about 150 to 200 metres away, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And when you say "away," are you referring away from the Markale market?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I'm referring to a distance between the place where the shell exploded and the Markale.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And just to confirm, you indicated that the third shelling took place between about 30 and 50 metres from the Markale market. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. A third shell hit the same street, Mula Mustafe Baseskije, which was then known as Marsal Tito Street. And the distance between the place where it exploded and Markale market is not more than 30 metres. If anything, it is probably less than 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. In your statement, you certainly have a strong opinion as to what was occurring with these shellings. And you indicate that those opinions are based on the fact that you had been a mortar platoon commander in the JNA. I'd like to explore that a little bit with you. Can you please tell me when were you in the JNA, as a mortar commander?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I served in the JNA in 1980, in Banja Luka, and there, I was first trained as a soldier; then a non-commissioned officer; and then I was assigned to be a commander of a platoon; and, finally, when I left the army what was written in my military booklet was that I was a commander of the mortar platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What training did you receive in order to become a mortar commander?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: First, I operated the 82-millimetre mortar, and then I became a non-commissioned officer. I was a corporal. Then I was first trained as a platoon commander. But when I worked on mortar, I was operating the sight -- the sighting device.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And that's what I'm trying to explore a bit about. Can you please tell us what kind of education or training did you undergo in order to hold these positions?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I had to undergo a complete training. I had to get familiar with the weaponry, its use, and then I had to practice targeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you say you were practicing targeting, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: That means that we practiced with shells, real shells. We were given a target, and we were supposed to hit it. That's what we were trained to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How does one go about hitting a target?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: There is a rule how you determine the angle, the distance. You are trained how to hit a target by calculating your angle and by calculating the distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In regards to the succession of these three shells that we were discussing before, how -- what was the time-frame in which all three hit?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The three shells fell within about half an hour from each other. If the first one exploded around 10.00, then the third one probably exploded around 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: With the lining of these as well as the timing, is that consistent with the experience that you had sighting mortar, in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: It all depends on what you want to achieve, what you're aiming for, and within what time. In any case, this was ample time to correct fire in order to hit a target. According to our experience in Sarajevo, what happened was one shell would fall, then a certain period of time would pass, fire would be corrected, and the subsequent shell would inflict more casualties.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Based on your investigation of those three shellings, was a determination made in regards to the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The shells came from the direction of Lukavica, or Vraca in the Trebevic sector -- or, rather, from the slope of Trebevic, not from its top and the slopes of Trebevic is where the neighbourhood of Lukavica was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who controlled that territory?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Again, the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. I would now like to move to air bombs. You indicated in your statement that you had some experience in relation to those. Can you please tell me when is the first time that you encountered an air bomb in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date when that happened. However, we had received information that in the canyon of Muscanice [phoen] river, a modified rocket had fallen. We didn't know what this was all about. And when we went to the site we found an air bomb which had been modified, to carry four more rocket motors. And I believe that this had been fired from a multi-rocket-launcher. It never exploded. It just fell between some rocks. And the ignition device missed and failed to activate. I know that after that, people who were experts in explosives managed to take out about 90 kilos of explosives from that unexploded bomb.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What kind of damage can 90 kilos of explosive do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this witness is qualified to supply an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, based upon his experience of being a commander in a mortar unit he would certainly -- should certainly be able to answer, and if he wouldn't, he would, I believe, advise us of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that his experience with a mortar platoon has nothing in common with an air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as we've heard testimony repeatedly that an air bomb merely is a mortar with rockets attached to it. The load, the specific explosive load is related to the mortar aspects of which he would be experienced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a more fundamental problem, Madam Carter. And it doesn't arise on there question only. It has arisen a couple of minutes ago. You're leading this witness like is he an expert witness. Is he an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. However, he has given opinions, lay opinions within his witness statement. And I'm just trying to provide the context in which he is making them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And precisely because of that, what's the law about opinions of laypeople? Are they admissible?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: They certainly are admissible; however, the Court would not rely upon them the same way as they would rely upon an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do laypeople give opinion evidence, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think people give their opinions all the time in regards to what happened. We can't put ourselves in the mind of the people who are firing upon us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about what people do. I'm asking you about the law. Does the law say laypeople give opinion evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would have to fully brief that, Your Honour. I know it has been the practice of the cases in which I have been a part of, that they have been allowed to give opinion evidence. As to what their basic experience is, they certainly would not be able to then extrapolate on some other area of Sarajevo or some other incident that he didn't have personal knowledge about. And that's what makes the difference. An expert able to extrapolate on things that he didn't have personal dealings with, as opposed to this witness is merely talking about those matters which he did deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But did he deal with determining the amount of damage that a 90-kilo air bomb can cause? Did he deal with that 90-kilo air bomb that was there, that he found -- that was found in the rocks?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: He is indicating that he certainly did. And given the fact that he was responsible for many investigations in regards to sniping and shelling within Sarajevo, I believe that he would be in a position to be able to answer that question. However, I can withdraw it if the court feels that it is not helpful to its determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think it is very helpful, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, outside of this air bomb, did you encounter any others during your time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Well, we conducted on-site investigations of all shells which landed and exploded in the territory of our municipality. So from gun rounds, 82-millimetres, mortars, Howitzers, 120-millimetres, mortar shells, and so on. And I know that great damage was caused especially when it comes to large-calibre mortar shells. At that point in time, when we would arrive on site, what was really important us was to establish the direction of firing, and that indicated that this shell had been fired in the direction of Stari Grad, old town.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd actually like to move back to the question. We know that your statement, that you did investigate one air bomb. Is that the only air bomb that you encountered during your time in Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Based on the investigation of that air bomb, do you have any information as regards to who fired?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, we, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did not have such weaponry. So these air bombs could only have been fired from the positions under the control of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You just indicated "we," in relation to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Were you a member of the military, or were you a member of the police force?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No. I was a member of police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All right. Now I would like to move back to the incident that took place in the flea market. Sir, did you assist in the investigation of that flea market shelling?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the team which conducted on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. When you say you were part of a team, who makes up that team?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: There was an investigating judge, who led the investigation, was in charge of it; then there were officials from the homicide unit of the Sarajevo cantonal MUP; and then there were crime technicians from the Sarajevo cantonal MUP; and also officials from the crime prevention unit of Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Which type of individual were you, in relation to that investigation?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: When there is a shelling incident, it is usually the uniformed policemen who secure the location. Following that, an on-site investigation team usually arrives, led by an investigating judge. Our task, my colleague and I, who represented the Stari Grad police, were there to work under the orders of the investigating judge to locate the traces of explosion, traces of a shell that had exploded, and then following that, crime technicians would arrive to take photographs of the site. And then on the orders of the police, that would be secured and isolated, and analysis would be conducted, and then the entire material would be forwarded to the investigating judge for further proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And just to make sure I know where in that answer your role ended, you indicated that you were to look for the traces of explosion, traces of a shell that had exploded. Now is that your entire role? And then somebody else takes on the job from there?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the official reports that are drawn up, based on this type of investigation?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: A judge is in charge of it, and then a report is drawn up by the police officials from the homicide unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would ask that 65 ter number 1439B be brought up into e-court. And I believe Defence counsel is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that we have not received an answer to the question that was just put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Are you interested in getting the answer, ma'am, or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We just want to know, are you interested?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I thought he had answered. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with the types of reports that are drawn up after an investigation such as this?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And I would ask that this exhibit be taken to page 2 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I see on the official report, there is a listing of ten individuals who worked on this investigation, with your name following as number 10. Are you familiar with the other gentlemen who took part in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And during your proofing session, did you have the opportunity to review this file?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Do you believe that this file is a true and accurate depiction of the investigation that was performed in relation to the 22 December 1994 shelling incident?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I am seeking to tender this document. However, I do want to bring the Court's attention to the fact that P415 is also a copy of this file. The English version is complete in both 415 as well as in 65 ter 1439B. The discrepancy comes in with regards to the B/C/S. The original exhibit P415 only contains 11 pages of the B/C/S. We had asked for guidance and received it that we could not add those additional pages to the exhibit because it actually had already been tendered and accepted by the Court. So I would request that -- that these two exhibits be merged so that we have a complete B/C/S and English copy, and would certainly, for clarity of the record, like to maintain it as P415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't got a problem with it, Your Honour. Whatever is the best technical solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, is this exhibit in both English and B/C/S complete? This one. This one here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The one before you is complete, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Complete on both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, this document here is admitted in its entirety. Will it please replace Exhibit P415 -- and Exhibit P415 be withdrawn completely, and this take the number P415.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And at this time, the Prosecution passes the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Just a moment please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dozo, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am Defence counsel Novak Lukic, and I will be examining you on behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Perisic. I would kindly ask you to pause a bit before giving your answer, and I will do the same before putting a new question so that the interpreters can follow us.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to put a few questions to you concerning what I will call the first incident, in Sedrenik where Selmanovic, Dervisa was injured. At that time, you worked at the Stari Grad police station. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your exact job position at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I was an inspector in the crime prevention police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, within your scope of duties, were you authorised to file criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These criminal reports or criminal complaints are normally sent to the public prosecutor who has jurisdiction over it.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your police station received information that in Sedrenik a woman was injured, and at that time a team was set up within the police station, which was to go to the location and to carry out an on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How is such a team established or set up at the police station?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Once we receive information about an incident, the head of the shift within the police station informs a judge about the incident. Following that the cantonal MUP, which had technical equipment to cover the entire city of Sarajevo and then within the forensics department, they had a KDZ unit where there were ballistics experts working. The judge would then authorise an inspector to go to the site if he, the judge, wasn't able to go himself, and it would be the police inspector from the police station in the territory where the incident happened. Once the on-site investigation is completed, then the inspector is duty-bound to draw up the minutes or the report of the on-site investigation, to complete it with photographs and to deliver all of that together to the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, the ballistics expert who joins you, together with forensics experts, they come from the cantonal MUP?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, it is the cantonal MUP, the CSB of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How much time normally elapse from the moment you learn of an incident -- if you remember in this particular case, how much time was needed for a team to be set up and to arrive at the site?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The setting up of the team itself was not a problem, but it was a problem to go to the location, because there would be additional shellings, usually. And sometimes it would take us two, three, four hours before we were able to get to the location. Sometimes a judge wasn't available because he was busy with other grave cases. And in those instances he would authorise an inspector to go instead of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this particular case the officer on duty at the police station was informed that this woman had been injured in her left leg.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And armed with this information, you went to the site?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the site you did not find this injured woman?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You learned that she had been transported to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there, at the location, the neighbours described the incident to you.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And they described to you where she stood when the incident happened.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. And we found some blood in that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't take any statements from them, did you?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't manage to reach the location because of the shooting that was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. We were taking shelter behind the house where Mrs. Selmanovic lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it was only from that location that you were able to take photographs of the -- of the location where you had been informed she had been injured?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many photographs were made on the occasion, photographs of the actual site?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember later on, when you officially interviewed Mrs. Selmanovic, did you show her the photographs of the site?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ask her to draw a sketch of the place where she had been injured?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when the on-site investigation was conducted, the ballistics expert and the forensic technicians, what were doing?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: They were taking photographs of the site. And based on the accounts of neighbours, we tried to establish where the shooting had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And based on the accounts of neighbours, you obtained information that you then recorded in the on-site investigation report?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, you never interviewed or took statements from those people.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No. We didn't manage to. We were not able to take statements from the people right there on the location. We had to tell them to come to the police station. And it was war-time, and it was difficult for people to come to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there a number of such cases where you drew up on-site investigation reports without taking statements from eye-witnesses?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the ballistics expert who was present wrote a report? Normally he does that when his finding is requested.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Ballistics experts and forensic technicians were not from my police station; they were from the cantonal MUP. So they never provided any reports to me. At least I didn't see any reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The person who files a criminal complaint or report, isn't that person duty-bound to collect all documents that accompany such a report?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: At the time we did not file criminal reports against unknown perpetrators. It was something that an investigating judge was supposed to do, because he would later receive all the relevant documentation, together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you provided your portion of the paperwork, the Official Note, and the report, you provided that three months later, and you supposed that the ballistics expert and the forensic technicians provided their reports?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you had no idea about what they had written in their reports?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From there you went to the hospital, you found a doctor, on duty, you entered his name in to your Official Note. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid any confusion -- just bear with me for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce Exhibit P1939. And can we please zoom in on the bottom part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this is a note on the on-site inspection of the incident that took place on the 9th of December 1994?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says here in the penultimate paragraph she was transported by a vehicle to the Kosevo clinical Hospital, and there she received medical assistance at the orthopaedic department. She was sent home for treatment after her wound had been dressed. According to Dr. Fuad Dzankovic her wound was not serious. Has this jogged your memory, do you remember now that you spoke to the doctor who was on duty at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When we completed our investigation, we went to the hospital to look for the lady. And the doctor had admitted here was able to ascertain that the wound was not serious, and he discharged her.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ask the doctor to provide you with a report about the nature of her wounds?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No. At the time nobody did that. We did not ask for medical findings. The medical findings were given to the lady, and she took them with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ask the doctor to show you anything in writing about the type of wound and what leg was wounded?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I only remember that at the time that he told us that it was a slight injury, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you inform him that your information -- according to your information it was the left leg.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we with scroll up just a little. I have one more question. It will be brief. For that, I would like to see the upper portion of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This on-site investigation report was compiled two days post festum?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. On the 14th of December and the -- and the incident took place on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the information about the wounded including the address Zaima Sarca Street, who did you receive that from?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Probably from the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce P1940.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Three months subsequently you were able to find the wounded woman, not before. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you interviewed her at the police station?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document shows that he -- that she was residing at the same address that you entered into your investigation report.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: However, the house number in this document is 57; whereas in the previous report, there was no number because we were not aware of the number of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you try in the meantime to go and look up her neighbours and ask for their opinion an information?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: They did not reside there, not all of them resided there at the time. The times were dangerous. It was dangerous to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you didn't go to Sedrenik once again to check on her?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The uniform police were in charge of that. They were in charge of the area, and they were in charge of inspecting, and they were supposed to find out whether the lady had returned to her former address in Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this a Sedrenik address? I apologise for asking. Are you familiar with this name?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The street is Sedrenik or, rather, the Zaim Sarca Street, and it does not depict a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, it is in the Sedrenik neighbourhood; is it not?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The Zaim Sarca Street is in centre municipality, not in Sedrenik. Close to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When she told you that she had been wounded in the right leg, which you then recorded in your Official Note, did you send that information to the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. By way of an Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And again you didn't obtain any medical records to that effect?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No, I didn't. It is possible that -- that it does say so in the report, but I don't remember that we had a camera or that we scanned the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in something else that makes part of the procedure. When your police station is informed that an incident happened, you record some information, and on this particular occasion the information that you recorded was that she was wounded in the left leg. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When information is obtained subsequently, is that information entered in the log-book as well?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: You're talking about the day in the log-book of daily events. And if you're referring to that, we don't enter any subsequent information into that daily log-book, the log-book of daily events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What you are saying is this: If the original information entered into the log-book is that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see in the transcript that there's now an indication that we cannot distinguish between the question and the answer. I would ask -- I suppose, it's a slowing-down issue. And also can we get some differentiation, so we know who to attribute whatever lines were at issue to either witness or to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Counsel and witness, can be please slow down and make sure you pause between each other's speeches. Madam Carter is asking that we attribute words to people I'm not quite sure whether you are able to do that, but if you are, please do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters. I have tried to bear their work in mind, and I will try to control myself and make the transcript as legible as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, if the original information is obtained and entered into the log-book, and if according to that information, somebody was killed and if it is learned subsequently that the original information was not correct, the log-book, the original record in the log-book is not subsequently corrected. Is that what you have told us?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: It cannot happen that somebody got killed and that this -- that such information is misrecorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me be a bit more precise. There is a log-book at the police station and somebody calls in and says that there was an incident with casualties, with somebody who got killed. That is a possibility?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A team is sent to the site, they carry out an on-site inspection and they obtain different information. Is the original information corrected in the log-book that is kept at the station?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: There's so little room in the log-book that you can only record the original information that was obtained, that came in. If there are drastic consequences, if a shell fell with a number of wounded, that is recorded. At a later stage, three or four months later after many such incidents happened, we never went back to subsequently change the original data because the person who originally obtained the information would have to record the subsequent information -- information could be recorded by every officer on duty. The only valid document was an Official Note, which was then submitted to the prosecutor. And that was the only valid document that we always went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's correct. And only based on that document, one could know how many people were indeed killed, or about reasonable suspicion that somebody was killed.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Based on people calling in, we made a record of that person's name, the person who called in, and then we recorded the information that we obtained, especially if somebody got killed, because we also had to inform the families of the people who were allegedly killed. We also conducted hospital, morgues in order to ascertain whether it was that particular person, that was really in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that according to your information, in the area of Sedrenik, between 50 and 100 people fell victim to sniping incidents. That's what you have told us.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Sniping incidents and shelling combined, I believe. That would be better said. This was not the only incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know and you participated in only one more case, where one man had been hit by a sniper. That's what you testified.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. And that person also died. I went to some on-site inspections where there were no human casualties involved, but there was damages to the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're talking about human victims because that's part of your testimony, and that's part of what has been recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to the Dervisa Selmanovic case, you personally participated in one more incident that involved human casualties in that area.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. The second incident was the one during which a man had been killed, but I also participated in on-site investigations after sniper fire had been opened on houses, but such incidents did not involve any dead. There were people injured, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also did not have an insight into the book that could confirm your statement that between 50 and 100 people got killed in that area.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: That's because I never carried out any private investigations of my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. We're testifying about the facts here. That's why I'm asking you only about the facts. You can't tell the Trial Chamber the name of any other person who was killed or in that area during the war?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: After so many years, I really can't remember the name of the person who got killed in the incident that I investigated personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The figure that you gave us is part of your assumption. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: From the moment the aggression started to the moment the country was reintegrated, there was no single day without sniper fire from Spicaste Stijena. And every day people got targeted and killed in Sedrenik, not only from sniper fire but also from shelling by mortars and Howitzers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you very specifically whether you are aware of any other incidents besides the two that you participated in. Are you aware of any other concrete incident, victim or a colleague of yours who participated in an investigation of a very concrete incident?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I can't remember any.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple more questions about this topic. As far as I could understand, when you described the positions of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sedrenik in relation to Spicaste Stijena, you said that it was impossible for the shots to have come from the positions of the BiH army, because in that case their backs would be turned to Spicaste Stijena?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No. Spicaste Stijena is an elevation about 900 metres above the sea level, and that's -- hence its name. And below Spicaste Stijena there is an rock and there's a meadow under that, and there you have this neighbourhood or settlement. There were no positions of the BiH army there, because it would have been too close. And the positions would have been at the foot of Spicaste Stijena, and that would be about 20 metres distance from the very top. So they could have thrown rocks at them. That's why the lines were moved left to Grdonja. And in the right direction the positions were moved to a forest, the name of which I don't know. That's where the lines were. But they were not exactly lines; they were just two or three positions or protective bunkers of sorts that protected the area from the onslaught of Serb forces towards Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, how far away is Spicaste Stijena from Sedrenik or the location where that lady got wounded?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: It is very close. I can't tell you exactly how close, but maybe, as the crow flies, not more than 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The positions of the BH army in Sedrenik as far as I could understand, were mostly manned by the locals, by people who resided there.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: 90 per cent were those people or somebody else. If the line had to be reinforced, somebody would come from different areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They were armed. Did they also have uniforms; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Some did, and some were there in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, when they were not on positions, they resided in Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Some lived in Sedrenik, and the others lived in town. It all depended on how resourceful they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this is a good time for -- to end our session today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, unfortunately, we have to knock off, but we are not done with you. Can you, please, come back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 again in the afternoon in the same courtroom. And I warn that you while you are still giving evidence, you may not discuss the case with anybody, not even with your lawyers, okay. Thank you so much. Court adjourned tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of March, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24
